Prediction target period: from 2025-10-06 to 2025-10-21. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A significant fire broke out at the Novelis aluminum rolling plant in Oswego, New York, on the night of September 16, 2025, causing substantial disruption to the U.S. automotive industry. [2, 4, 12] The blaze, which drew a response from 26 fire departments and 175 firefighters, severely damaged the facility's hot mill, a critical area for producing aluminum sheet, and led to a partial roof collapse. [2, 4, 10] No injuries were reported among plant employees or first responders. [4, 5] The Oswego plant is a crucial supplier, accounting for approximately 40% of the aluminum sheet used by U.S. automakers. [3, 4, 10] The production halt has significantly impacted companies like Ford, which heavily relies on this aluminum for its best-selling F-150 pickup truck, as well as General Motors, Stellantis, and Toyota. [3, 6, 9] Analysts projected that the disruption could result in a financial hit to Ford of between $500 million and $1 billion. [6, 10] In response, Novelis has been sourcing materials from its overseas plants and collaborating with other suppliers to mitigate the shortfall, though this faces challenges from a 50% U.S. tariff on imported aluminum. [2, 3] The incident has also put upward pressure on domestic aluminum prices, with the Midwest Premium reaching a record high. [7] Novelis expects to restart the damaged hot mill in early 2026. [4, 6, 9] <2> On September 12, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced a proposal to eliminate the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP). Established in 2009, this program mandates that over 8,000 industrial facilities and suppliers across 47 source categories report their annual greenhouse gas emissions. The EPA's stated rationale for the proposal is to reduce regulatory burdens and save American businesses up to $2.4 billion in compliance costs, arguing the program is not directly tied to a potential regulation and does not materially improve health or the environment. If finalized, the rule would end reporting obligations for 46 of the 47 source categories. Reporting requirements for the remaining category, petroleum and natural gas systems, would be suspended until 2034. Opponents of the proposal, including environmental groups, argue that eliminating the program would remove a critical source of transparent and comparable emissions data used by regulators, industries, and the public, potentially making it more difficult and expensive to address climate change. <3> In a report released in September 2025, the Aluminum Association announced that North American (U.S. and Canada) aluminum demand decreased by 4.4% year-over-year for the first half of 2025. Total demand was an estimated 13.1 billion pounds through June 2025, a decline from 13.7 billion pounds in the first half of 2024. The primary driver of this decline was a significant drop in exports, though demand fell in all market segments except for foil. Specifically, shipments of aluminum ingot for castings, exports, and destructive uses fell by 11%, while aluminum mill products contracted by 1.6%. In contrast, imports of aluminum and aluminum products increased by 15.8% year-over-year, and aluminum scrap inventory grew by 14.7%, a trend the association attributes to tariff policies. Charles Johnson, president & CEO of the Aluminum Association, stated, “We are carefully monitoring the market as more data becomes available on how the current tariff landscape is impacting the industry,” emphasizing the need for trade policies that support the U.S. aluminum industry. <4> The Associated General Contractors of America (AGC), in an analysis of government data, reported that the producer price index (PPI) for construction materials saw significant year-over-year increases as of August 2025. Specifically, the PPI for aluminum mill shapes rose by 22.8% over the 12-month period, while also increasing 5.5% in August alone. This was part of a broader trend of accelerating costs, with notable price hikes for steel mill products and lumber as well. The AGC attributed these "extreme" price increases in large part to tariffs, which enabled domestic producers to raise their prices. Tariffs on steel and aluminum had been raised to 50% on June 4, and a 50% tariff on many copper products took effect on August 1. The rising costs led some contractors to raise their own prices and resulted in project cancellations or delays. <5> A market analysis from the Shanghai Metal Market (SMM) on September 1, 2025, concluded that aluminum prices were more likely to rise than fall during the month. [2] This optimistic forecast was attributed to significant macroeconomic support, including strong market expectations for a U.S. Federal Reserve interest rate cut and China's implementation of policies designed to boost domestic demand. [2] While the report noted that the translation of these policies into actual consumption would take time and that consumption had only shown marginal improvement in early September, other fundamental factors provided price support. [2] These included total inventory levels not being high and potential production declines in some Chinese provinces, where certain secondary aluminum enterprises faced the termination of tax rebate policies, which could decrease capacity. [2] <6> On August 21, 2025, the United States and the European Union issued a joint statement detailing a framework for a bilateral trade agreement. Under this non-binding framework, the U.S. will maintain its 50% tariffs on EU steel, aluminum, and their derivative products. In a cooperative effort to address global overcapacity, particularly from China, the two parties announced their intention to explore tariff-rate quota (TRQ) solutions aimed at strengthening their domestic markets and securing bilateral supply chains. <7> Loftis Steel & Aluminum, a family-owned steel fabrication company based in Nashville, Tennessee, announced a $6.5 million investment to launch a new high-tech manufacturing facility in Decatur, Alabama. The project is expected to create 20 new jobs in Limestone County, with an average wage of nearly $28 per hour. The new operation will produce custom metal components for a wide range of commercial and industrial applications and will be equipped with advanced technologies, including state-of-the-art fiber lasers and precision cutting systems. Tom Russell, President and CEO of Loftis Steel & Aluminum, stated that Decatur's strategic proximity to their Nashville operations was a key factor in the site selection, as it provides a "springboard" to better serve the expanding North Alabama market. <8> A new 50% tariff on copper imports was announced by the United States in July 2025; While not directly on aluminum, this action is part of a broader series of tariff measures under the Trump Administration; this action is part of a broader series of tariff measures under the Trump Administration <9> Sachin Shivaram, CEO of Wisconsin Aluminum Foundry, has publicly stated that recent tariffs on aluminum imports are creating a competitive disadvantage and negatively impacting his business. The tariffs have led to a significant increase in input costs for the company, which relies on imported primary aluminum due to the high domestic energy costs associated with its production. This cost increase has been passed on to customers. Shivaram mentioned losing an order to a Canadian competitor whose aluminum costs are substantially lower. He also noted a rapid decline in manufacturing demand since the tariffs were announced and indicated that the company has had to lay off workers at its plants. While expressing that the idea behind the tariffs could be beneficial, Shivaram criticized the rollout as chaotic and urged for a more permanent strategy developed in consultation with trade associations.
